content:
Achilles Expands Global Supply Chain With Cm3 Acquisition
Prioritise Us
Achilles is strengthening its global presence and leadership in supply chain intelligence with movement to the APAC region, following an acquisition of Cm3
In today's world, organisations are doing what they can to drive resilience, as
ongoing volatility
creates shocks around global supply chains.
supply chain risk
and performance management, Achilles, is focusing on growing its capabilities and expanding its presence, working to strengthen its position in the market.
Conversations about how to improve competitiveness and conduct successful transformations will be taking place at  Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September.
Secure your ticket today
to ensure you do not miss out.
For our customers, the value lies in uniting two organisations that share an identical model for success: cutting-edge technology, deep domain expertise, and a service-led approach.
Achilles’ CEO, Sebastien Roussotte
, an organisation which helps businesses increase efficiency, reduce risk and improve sustainability, has announced plans to acquire Cm3. Achilles has signed an agreement to acquire the platform. Cm3 is a trusted partner, offering software services for contractor management in the Australian market.
This is part of Achilles' international growth strategy, as it has already conducted a series of acquisitions across Spain, Argentina and the US. Now, it is expanding its capabilities in contractor compliance, supplier assurance and ongoing supply chain intelligence.
Achilles aims to increase confidence in decision-making, particularly about suppliers and third parties. It also works alongside suppliers to help them improve their performance. The aim is to strengthen compliance, capability and resilience across global supply chains, using continuous monitoring, verified data, active supplier engagement and a connected network.
Through this, it works to build more resilient supply chains, actively addressing the gaps rather than simply helping organisations understand supplier risk. The acquisition will help it gain more ground in Australia, as Cm3 is already a trusted partner in driving contractor compliance, workforce safety and operational risk management. Through modern technology and human expertise, contractor management operates as a streamlined process with high standards of compliance,
competency and safety
“Achilles’ agreement to acquire Cm3 marks a major milestone in building a truly global supply chain risk management partner for businesses operating across complex, international networks," explains Sebastien Roussotte, CEO of Achilles, to Supply Chain Digital.
"For our customers, the value lies in uniting two organisations that share an identical model for success: cutting-edge technology, deep domain expertise, and a service-led approach. While intelligent software is critical, customers also require human expertise, local market knowledge and trusted advisory teams to navigate regulatory and operational risks effectively."
Achilles helps organisations gain ongoing visibility across their entire supply chain, including risk surveillance across suppliers, contractors and global third parties. The acquisition will expand Achilles' capabilities of helping organisations manage risk, using deep expertise in contractor compliance and Achilles' supply chain intelligence capabilities.
Organisations will be able to move beyond fragmented operations, which causes a lot of risk to global supply chains. In today's era of complex operations and high risk – driven by an increase in cyber attacks,
changing regulations and compliance standards
, volatility, unpassable trade routes, materials shortages and inflation – supply chain cohesion is a necessity.
Visibility across supply chains helps drive operational resilience, assurance and much greater risk management.
Sebastien explains; "The acquisition strengthens the value we can offer to customers operating across multiple markets. As supply chains become more international, more regulated and more exposed to disruption, customers increasingly need a partner that can combine local assurance with global reach.
"That is where we believe the combination of Achilles and Cm3 will create real value. Cm3 customers could, upon completion and regulatory approval, benefit from access to Achilles’ broader global supplier network, including our current base of more than 330,000 suppliers. Likewise, Achilles customers will gain access to Cm3’s established supplier and contractor network across Australia and New Zealand.
"For global companies managing complex supply chains, this creates a stronger platform for visibility, assurance and resilience in increasingly volatile supply chain landscape."

"One of the key benefits we can bring to Cm3 customers is Achilles’ investment in AI," adds Sebastien.
"We are investing in technology that helps customers move from fragmented, periodic checks to continuous supply chain intelligence. Cm3 is already focused on harnessing AI to make better use of the information it holds for customers, and we can help accelerate that progress by sharing our technology roadmap, data expertise and product investment."
The acquisition will help position Achilles more firmly into a global standing, with the expectation of closing the deal in the next few months, subject to regulatory approval. The deal shows ongoing growth for Achilles, demonstrating its competitiveness in the global market.

title: DP World: Developing Flexibility Across Global Trade Routes
content:
DP World: Developing Flexibility Across Global Trade Routes
Prioritise Us
DP World is expanding the UAE gateway network, with two new terminals at the Fujairah Ports Authority, working to drive greater connectivity in trade
is working to provide greater connectivity and flexibility to customers in UAE, through the expansion of the Fujairah Ports Authority.
Amid ongoing geopolitical volatility and disruption in the critical trade route of the
Strait of Hormuz
, logistics companies around the world are looking to better support their customers.
This new development will support UAE capacity growth and will help streamline global trade.
The Al Rugaylat and Dibba terminals will bring world-class operating capability, expanded capacity and new investment to the emirate.
H.H. Sheikh Saleh Bin Mohamed Al Sharqi, Chairman, Fujairah Ports Authority
The Port of Fujairah is the only multi-purpose seaport on the eastern coastline of UAE, located 70 nautical miles from the Strait of Hormuz. Due to this,it has been strategically located in order to provide essential access to trade. The port acts as an economic link between Europe and Asia, as well as providing more trade opportunities to India and North East Africa.
To increase operation capacity,
has developed an agreement with the Fujairah Ports Authority, to develop two new terminals, as part of a 50-year deal. The Al Rugaylat terminal is a multi-purpose and container terminal, and DP World will also operate the Dibba General Cargo terminal. DP World currently operates four ports and facilities in the UAE; Jebel Ali, Mina Al Hamriya, Mina Rashid and Dubai Creek & Deira Wharfage.
"Locating the new terminal outside the Straight of Hormuz would enable ships to sail in relative safety; the construction of the port was effectively a response to the closure of the Straight in the 1980s Iran-Iraq ware. However, the 12 May 2019 attack as well as more recent issues shows that it is not immune from danger," explains Emile Naus, Partner at BearingPoint in a statement to Supply Chain Digital.
The new terminals will create a deep-water trade gateway on the east coast of UAE, with capabilities of handling Ultra Large Container Vessels. Al Rugaylat will be able to handle up to 2.5 million TEUs every year, as well as 1.7 million tonnes of general cargo and 190,000 Car Equivalent Units (CEUs). Dibba will manage up to 3.6 million tonnes of annual general cargo capacity.
"The partnership with DP World marks an important milestone in Fujairah's continued development as one of the region's most important maritime gateways," says H.H. Sheikh Saleh Bin Mohamed Al Sharqi, Chairman, Fujairah Ports Authority.
"The Al Rugaylat and Dibba terminals will bring world-class operating capability, expanded capacity and new investment to the emirate. We look forward to working with DP World to deliver a project that will benefit customers, communities and the UAE's wider economy."
Construction is expected to take 24 to 30 months
Capacity for DP World in the UAE will reach 22 million TEUs
Al Rugaylat will handle 1.7 million tonnes of general cargo and 190,000 CEUs every year
Dibba will increase general cargo capacity by 3.6 million tonnes annually
The Port of Jebel Ali and the Port of Fujairah are 152 km apart by road
There are approximately 245 nautical miles between Jebel Ali Port and the Port of Fujairah
It is anticipated that the new logistics zone will drive further investment, employment and long-term economic opportunity to the region. Moreover, it will expand DP World's capabilities of supporting global trade.
Within the UAE, DP World currently has a total container handling capacity of 19.4 million TEUs, but with this expansion, it will reach almost 22 million TEUs. It will be able to deliver as a global integrated platform across global supply chains, with more capacity amid
growing demand
for trade. With the rise of ecommerce and a growing need of supply chain diversification, ports and terminals around the world are challenged with growing their operational capacity.
It offers greater choice of destination for cargo owners, as well as more flexibility when operating in periods of high demand, as well as more supply chain resilience amid global volatility.
"The UAE has been at the heart of DP World's story for more than four decades, and this investment reflects our confidence in its future as one of the world's leading trade and logistics hubs," explains H.E. Essa Kazim, Chairman, DP World.
"Building on the
strength of Jebel Ali
, this development deepens our commitment to the UAE and reinforces the country's strategic role in global trade."
As DP World operates as a multimodal logistics company, the Fujairah terminals will be connected to Jebel Ali through its inland logistics network. This allows for a more integrated end-to-end supply chain across the UAE, with
expanded capabilities
of moving cargo efficiently between ports, logistics hubs and end markets.
Emile, however, warns of logistics concerns which could occur within the new terminal, stating, "the port is more exposed than the existing Jebel Ali facilities, with direct exposure to the weather in the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea", and that due to its elevation, there are logistical issues regarding road freight.
However, he also points to the anticipated risk to Jebel Ali that DP World may be facing amid ongoing geopolitical turbulence.
Construction of these ports is anticipated to take 24 to 30 months.

title: EcoVadis & Schneider: Decarbonising Pharma Supply Chains
content:
EcoVadis & Schneider: Decarbonising Pharma Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
EcoVadis links its Responsible Health Initiative with Schneider Electric's Energize programme to boost supplier climate action in pharma supply chains
EcoVadis has confirmed a new collaboration between its Responsible Health Initiative (RHI) and the Energize programme.
Energize is designed and delivered by SE Advisory Services, which is Schneider Electric's global consulting practice.
The collaboration is intended to support
decarbonisation across pharmaceutical supply chains
. Suppliers linked to the RHI can now access training and guidance for climate action through Energize.
According to EcoVadis, Scope 3 emissions are 21 times larger than Scope 1 and Scope 2 combined for the average company.
The organisation states that ignoring these emissions could cost companies more than US$500bn in annual liabilities by 2030.
Within the healthcare sector specifically, EcoVadis reports that only 6% of companies have a plan in place to move toward
low-carbon operations and supply chains
This gap could mean there is scope for healthcare companies to develop emissions reduction plans and engage further with climate action.
Steve Wilhite, Executive Vice President at SE Advisory Services, writes on LinkedIn: "Supply chain decarbonisation is too complex for any one organisation to tackle alone. So we're celebrating a new milestone in our collaboration with EcoVadis.
"Suppliers participating in their Responsible Health Initiative can now join our Energize programme. Led by SE Advisory Services, the programme provides training for decarbonisation efforts across global pharmaceutical value chains.
"Bringing together healthcare leaders, suppliers and sustainability experts creates a powerful opportunity to address some of the most significant Scope 3 emissions challenges facing the industry. Collaboration remains one of the most effective ways to scale climate action."
The Responsible Health Initiative was founded in 2018 by a group of healthcare, biotech and pharmaceutical companies with the aim of advancing sustainability across their value chains.
The initiative allows industry leaders to share best practices and processes. This could foster common understanding between companies looking to improve sustainability performance.
Members aim to strengthen supplier outreach and expand visibility of the wider health sector's supply chain sustainability performance. The setup allows companies to engage directly with industry peers and external stakeholders.
Through the new collaboration, suppliers can build plans to transition toward renewable energy. The RHI also offers training and personalised guidance intended to help suppliers build confidence with carbon management and sustainability reporting.
Fernanda Campos Helmeister, Supply Chain Decarbonisation Programme Manager at SE Advisory Services, says: "The Responsible Health Initiative's new collaboration with SE Advisory Services's Energize programme makes renewable energy adoption much more accessible across geographies, supporting decarbonisation efforts across the pharma and healthcare value chain as a whole."
brings together 27 global pharmaceutical companies with the goal of engaging hundreds of suppliers in climate action.
The programme is focused on the decarbonisation of the pharmaceutical value chain.
Through the link with the RHI, suppliers can now join Energize to access education, digital tools and advisory services delivered by teams at Schneider Electric.
Sponsor companies involved in Energize include AstraZeneca, GSK, Haleon, Sanofi, Novo Nordisk, Johnson & Johnson and Novartis among others.
"As we confront the urgent reality of the climate crisis, we understand that collective action is essential," says Katiana Iavarone, Chief Procurement Officer at UCB, one of the sponsor companies.
"At UCB, we're committed to driving the ecological transition also through renewable energy. By forging key partnerships, such as the Energize programme, we strive to achieve significant decarbonisation outcomes and extend our impact beyond what we can achieve alone.
"Together, we're building a more sustainable future."
Executive Vice President

title: Orchestrating Supply Chains with Siemens & NVIDIA AI
content:
Orchestrating Supply Chains with Siemens & NVIDIA AI
Prioritise Us
Siemens and NVIDIA expand their collaboration to advance self-verifying agentic AI workflows ahead of Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September
With global supply chain leaders facing complexity and volatility at never before seen levels,
manual processes and fragmented digital designs
are becoming increasingly useless. To stay ahead of competitors, organisations are looking to speed up their transition towards end-to-end supply chain orchestration.
Orchestration enables companies to predict disruptions and respond automatically in real time, and leading technology innovators are bringing this concept into the hardware and engineering foundation of modern supply chains.
Siemens has announced its strategic collaboration with NVIDIA to introduce self-verifying agentic AI workflows. With this technology, it aims to streamline high-tech
manufacturing pipelines
and optimise component production.
Key Facts: What you need to know about the Siemens & NVIDIA partnership
Agentic AI integration: Siemens EDA and NVIDIA expanded their partnership at DAC 2026 to bring self-verifying agentic AI to semiconductor and PCB design.
Full-stack performance: Combining Siemens Fuse EDA with NVIDIA NeMo Gym, Nemotron models and CUDA-X accelerates library characterisation by more than 10x.
Self-verifying execution: Autonomous AI agents execute multi-step engineering tasks while validating outcomes against physics-based verification engines.
Enterprise security: Built on NVIDIA OpenShell to deliver sandboxed, secure execution with strict access controls and full auditability for hardware IP.
This new development comes as industry leaders prepare to gather at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit in September 2026 where they will discuss how advanced automation and orchestration
are reshaping the way we operate on a global scale.
secure your ticket now
to be part of this important conversation.
As part of the new collaboration between Siemens and NVIDIA, Siemens’s Fuse EDA AI Agent system will be paired with NVIDIA’s AI infrastructure to reshape semiconductor and printed circuit board (PCB) design workflows.
The next evolution of industrial AI relies on moving beyond autonomous task orchestration to continuously validated engineering outcomes.
Amit Gupta, Senior Vice President and Chief AI Strategy Officer at Siemens EDA
The platform equips AI agents with domain-specific intelligence by integrating the NVIDIA NeMo Gym open library and Nemotron open models. These autonomous agents can execute multi-step engineering tasks and reason through complex decisions, as well as learn from previous execution strategies.
“The next evolution of industrial AI relies on moving beyond autonomous task orchestration to continuously validated engineering outcomes,” says Amit Gupta, Senior Vice President and Chief AI Strategy Officer at Siemens EDA.
“By integrating NVIDIA AI infrastructure into our Fuse platform, we are giving our customers self-verifying AI agents that autonomously execute and prove their work against physics-based engines.”
Built on the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, the platform protects sensitive hardware IP while giving compliance teams full visibility and complete audit trails.
Boosted by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, design teams can reach signoff-quality results in hours rather than days. Lower token use and lighter computing demands also make it far cheaper to scale across large teams.
For high-tech supply chains, faster engineering convergence leads to shorter lead times and a more predictable manufacturing schedule. As semiconductor and hardware manufacturing networks become increasingly distributed, automated self-verification ensures multi-tier supplier operations maintain strict quality standards without manual intervention.
“Semiconductor and PCB design are among the most complex engineering challenges in the world, and AI agents need trusted tools to reason, act and verify their work,” says Timothy Costa, vice president and general manager of computational engineering at NVIDIA.
“Siemens is combining its EDA software with NVIDIA accelerated computing, AI software and Nemotron open models to create self-verifying agentic workflows that improve design quality, speed up results and give engineering teams greater confidence in every step of the process.”
As agentic AI becomes ever more integrated into physical engineering workflows, making sure interconnected networks run seamlessly requires design, procurement and logistics teams to all be on the same page.
This movement towards holistic supply chain orchestration will be a central topic at the

hosted by Supply Chain Digital and BizClik. The event takes place from 8 to 9 September 2026 at the QEII Centre in Westminster, London, UK.

More than 1,000 attendees and 50 expert speakers will explore how tools like agentic AI, advanced analytics and real-time tracking can build resilient supply chain ecosystems capable of navigating continuous global change.

title: BMW to launch series production of iX5 batteries in December - electrive.com
content:
The BMW Group is preparing to launch series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) batteries for electric vehicles – starting with high-voltage batteries for the
all-electric BMW iX5
, which will begin at its Woodruff plant this December. The facility is a cornerstone for the North American market and was built near the Spartanburg vehicle plant, where the iX5 will be manufactured, in line with the ‘Local for Local’ principle. From there, the vehicle will also be exported to Europe.
To achieve this, the carmaker has implemented cutting-edge processes. The new cylindrical cells in the 46120 format
are integrated directly into the battery pack using the ‘Cell-to-Pack’ method. All production steps are monitored seamlessly in real time. Specially developed AI assistants process data alongside more than 300 employees and 250 robots to ensure zero-defect production.
Even during the planning and ramp-up phases, BMW consistently relied on digital tools. Digital twins and virtual reality applications facilitated factory planning, while employees completed a specially developed VR training programme. This allowed them to practice real-world processes and equipment operations in a highly detailed virtual environment.
“Plant Woodruff plays a key role in the ramp-up of electromobility in the US,” said BMW Production Director Raymond Wittmann. “With our Gen6 high-voltage battery, we’re not only taking a major technological leap – we are also setting new standards in production. In Woodruff, we are combining cutting-edge processes, artificial intelligence and the expertise of our employees to create a production facility designed for the highest quality.”
These AESC cylindrical cells in the 46120 format are integrated into BMW battery systems
Technologically, the system is based on an 800-volt architecture. The BMW iX5 60 xDrive offers a usable net energy content of 144kWh in the USA and 141kWh in Europe. In terms of sustainability, the Gen6 battery cell reduces CO₂e emissions by around 28 per cent compared to the previous generation. This reduction is achieved through the use of secondary materials for cobalt, lithium, and nickel, as well as green electricity in cell production. The Woodruff plant itself operates entirely without fossil fuels during normal operations, while its material handling equipment is powered by hydrogen.
The foundation for the project was laid in June 2023 with the
groundbreaking ceremony for the Woodruff plant
. Construction commenced in September 2023, followed by the installation of equipment in autumn 2024. Pre-series test runs began in summer 2025. The investments in Woodruff are part of a comprehensive US strategy, in which BMW invested approximately $1.7 billion in electromobility in the Spartanburg region, including partnerships with local cell suppliers such as AESC.

title: Gotion eyes stake in PowerCo’s Spanish battery cell factory - electrive.com
content:
VW subsidiary PowerCo's battery cell factory in Spain could soon become a joint venture with Gotion before construction is even complete. According to a Spanish media report, VW is considering bringing its Chinese stakeholder on board at the site near Valencia.
This is what PowerCo's cell factory in Sagunt is expected to look like
Image: Volkswagen
As reported by the Spanish trade publication
La Tribuna de Automoción
, the Volkswagen Group is currently in advanced negotiations with its partner Gotion regarding the acquisition of a majority stake in the battery cell factory under construction in Sagunto, which – being near Valencia – PowerCo refers to as Gigafactory Valencia. According to sources, discussions have advanced well, and the Chinese group’s CEO, Zhen Li, has reportedly made high-level visits to the site.
At the heart of negotiations – which are being led by VW’s Board Member for Technology, Thomas Schmall – is the establishment of a joint venture. Under this arrangement, Gotion would take control of the Valencia plant, while PowerCo would remain as a minority shareholder. For Volkswagen, the factory is strategically indispensable, as it is to supply the company’s Spanish and Portuguese vehicle plants with the
Unified Cell
for EVs – which is already in production in Salzgitter.
A potential partnership between VW, PowerCo, and Gotion is not new to the industry. Volkswagen is the largest shareholder in the Chinese company, holding around a quarter of its shares, and Gotion ranks among the global top five battery cell manufacturers. However, as the battery cell factory in Sagunto is not yet operational, Gotion currently supplies cells for models produced in Spain, such as the
, from its factory in Hefei, China. Series production of the Unified Cell
began there in November 2025
. Previously, Gotion had served as a technology partner for the development of the Unified Cell and the construction of PowerCo’s cell production facility in Salzgitter, which reportedly involved hundreds of Chinese specialists.
If Gotion’s entry into the project succeeds, it could expand the customer base of the Valencia factory. According to industry sources, Gotion aims to supply other automotive manufacturers in Spain in the future, with Ford’s plant in Almussafes mentioned as a potential customer. This comes as the Chinese carmaker Geely is currently
planning to take a stake
in the plant.
Meanwhile, the Sagunto project is facing delays. According to sources, the start of pre-series production has been pushed back to December 2026, while series production was not expected to begin before summer 2027. Additionally, staff recruitment is behind schedule: currently, only 50 of the 500 employees required for pre-series production have been hired. PowerCo España declined to comment on market speculation but emphasised to
La Tribuna de Automoción
its unwavering commitment to the site and its swift implementation.
In response to an inquiry from
Automobilwoche
, PowerCo stated that it “regularly reviews strategic opportunities, including potential collaborations with partners.” A spokesperson added: “However, we have no plans to relinquish control of Gigafactory Valencia. PowerCo is fully committed to the Gigafactory in Sagunto and will continue to drive its development at pace.” This statement does not rule out Gotion’s involvement in the project but suggests that PowerCo would retain a majority stake in such a scenario.
Regardless of developments in Sagunto, Gotion is also advancing its plans for a
factory in Valladolid, Spain
. Following recent funding approvals under the Perte-VEC programme, a facility for cathodes and battery recycling is set to be established first.
about „Gotion eyes stake in PowerCo’s Spanish battery cell factory“

title: Rock Tech secures fixed buyer for Canadian lithium - electrive.com
content:
Rock Tech Lithium has signed a binding offtake agreement with Geneva-based commodity trader Transamine for its Georgia Lake project in Ontario. The partnership secures the commercial marketing of the lithium mined there and includes prepayment financing of up to $80 million USD.
Analysis of spodumene from the Georgia Lake project under the UV laser
Image: Stark Resources
The agreement covers the entire planned production of the Georgia Lake project in Ontario. From 2028, Rock Tech Lithium will supply Transamine with up to 100,000 dry metric tonnes of spodumene concentrate annually over an initial seven-year term. This concentrate is a powder produced from spodumene ore mined on-site, which contains a high proportion of lithium oxide (typically around 6 per cent). Battery-grade lithium for electric vehicles can be extracted from it in further processing steps.
The agreement includes a variable delivery volume. In the initial months of the contract, 50,000 tonnes are planned, before the volume increases to the annual maximum of 100,000 tonnes during regular operations. Pricing is based on internationally recognised market benchmarks for spodumene concentrate. The parties have also agreed on an option to extend the contract by up to five additional years.
A key element of the contract is the option for further processing. Rock Tech reserves the right to refine the spodumene concentrate into battery-grade chemicals at its
planned lithium converter in Red Rock
(near the Canadian mine). In such a case, the agreement would convert into a take-or-pay contract for lithium hydroxide or lithium carbonate with Transamine.
To support project development, Transamine is providing an upfront payment facility of up to $80 million USD. Disbursement is subject to strict conditions, including securing full equity financing for the project and obtaining all environmental and operational permits.
CEO Mirco Wojnarowicz describes the contract as a strategic milestone: “This agreement demonstrates how Rock Tech is turning critical minerals ambition into execution. It provides a long-term, commercial foundation for the Georgia Lake mine’s future production, strengthens our financing pathway, and – together with the prepayment facility – brings us another step closer to building the integrated mine-to-converter platform with the flexibility to convert raw material into battery-grade lithium chemicals through our Red Rock Lithium Converter.”
Repayment of the upfront payment will be made over a 24-month period from the first commercial delivery through direct offsetting against the concentrate volumes. Any remaining balances after this period must be settled in cash.
Rock Tech Lithium is active not only in Canada but also in Germany. In Germany, the company does not plan to mine lithium itself but instead aims to build a lithium converter in Guben, Brandenburg. However, the major hurdle for constructing the planned facility lies in the expected investment costs of €750 million euros – and as we saw recently, the young company
cannot shoulder this on its own
. Production was originally scheduled to start in 2027, but realistically, 2029 is now the earliest feasible date. The targeted production volume is expected to suffice for around 30GWh of battery capacity or approximately 500,000 EVs per year.

title: How the Shahed-136 became one of the world's most influential drones
content:
Few weapons have become as recognizable in modern warfare as the Shahed-136. With its distinctive delta-wing shape and unmistakable buzzing engine, the Iranian-designed loitering munition has become a defining feature of conflicts in recent years, particularly in Ukraine.
Despite its relatively simple design, it has sparked global discussions about the future of aerial warfare, air defense, and the economics of modern combat. So why has this comparatively inexpensive weapon attracted so much attention?
Although it is commonly referred to as a “drone,” the Shahed-136 is more accurately classified as a loitering munition or one-way attack UAV. Unlike reusable unmanned aircraft that return to base after completing surveillance or strike missions, the Shahed-136 is designed to locate its target and destroy itself on impact. In effect, the aircraft itself becomes the weapon.
Once launched, it follows pre-programmed navigation before diving into its target with an explosive warhead. This relatively simple concept eliminates the need for recovery systems while allowing operators to launch large numbers of aircraft in coordinated attacks. Defense analysts at
RUSI classify
the Shahed-136 as a one-way attack UAV, noting that such systems have become an increasingly important component of modern missile and drone campaigns.
One reason the Shahed-136 has received so much attention is that it deliberately avoids complexity. The aircraft features a compact delta-wing airframe powered by a small piston engine that produces the characteristic buzzing sound frequently reported during attacks. Rather than relying on sophisticated stealth technology or high-performance jet engines, the design prioritizes simplicity, ease of production, and operational reliability.
More from Military
US builds $50M hypersonic payload hub ahead of schedule to speed Mach 5+ flight testing
Kratos delivers advanced ramjet engine technology for future US Army missiles
Russia’s latest 13,800-ton nuclear submarine to carry hypersonic cruise missiles
US missile defenses to get strengthened with new 4-fold THAAD propulsion expansion
US Navy warships to be built by partner shipyards under HII’s new strategy
The drone is launched from angled racks mounted on trucks or trailers, allowing multiple aircraft to be fired in quick succession. This mobile launch system enables operators to relocate rapidly after launch, making them more difficult to target. Its relatively straightforward construction also makes large-scale manufacturing easier than for many advanced cruise missiles.
Perhaps the Shahed-136’s biggest advantage is not its speed or firepower, but its cost-effectiveness. Modern surface-to-air missiles capable of intercepting incoming threats can cost hundreds of thousands, or even millions of dollars per interceptor. By comparison, loitering munitions like the Shahed-136 are widely regarded as significantly cheaper to manufacture.
This creates what military planners call a cost-exchange dilemma: defenders may be forced to use expensive
missiles to destroy comparatively inexpensive incoming weapons.
Rather than relying on a single highly sophisticated aircraft, attackers can launch large numbers simultaneously, forcing defenders to expend valuable interceptor missiles while increasing the likelihood that at least some drones will reach their targets.
The Shahed-136 first drew international attention after its use by Russia in Ukraine, but its significance has only grown during the ongoing
U.S. war on Iran
. This campaign shows that relatively simple one-way attack drones are no longer niche weapons. They have become integral to modern strike operations.
Rather than relying solely on
cruise or ballistic missiles
, Iran has repeatedly paired Shahed-type drones with other long-range weapons to complicate air-defense operations. The approach forces defenders to track and engage multiple kinds of threats simultaneously while increasing pressure on interceptor stockpiles.
At the same time, Russia has continued expanding domestic production of the Shahed-136, known locally as the
, demonstrating how militaries increasingly view mass-produced loitering munitions as a core component of long-range warfare.
Perhaps the Shahed-136’s greatest achievement is that it has changed how militaries think about cost. The ongoing war involving the United States, Israel, and Iran has most clearly highlighted the cost-exchange dilemma.
A relatively inexpensive Shahed drone can force defenders to fire interceptor missiles that may cost orders of magnitude more, particularly when attacks come in large waves alongside ballistic or cruise missiles. Analysts have argued that the challenge is no longer simply intercepting drones. It is doing so economically over a sustained campaign.
This reality has accelerated investment in cheaper counter-drone interceptors, electronic warfare systems, and directed-energy weapons, as militaries seek alternatives to relying exclusively on high-end missile defenses. In that sense, the Shahed-136’s greatest legacy may not be the targets it destroys, but the billions of dollars it has forced adversaries to spend defending against it.
The Shahed-136’s greatest contribution may not be its technology, but the questions it has forced militaries to ask.
For decades, air power was measured by faster aircraft, stealthier platforms, and increasingly sophisticated precision weapons. The Shahed-136 has demonstrated that battlefield influence can also come from the opposite approach. Relatively inexpensive, expendable systems are deployed in large numbers to overwhelm defenses and impose disproportionate costs on an adversary.
The ongoing wars have shown that modern air campaigns are no longer defined solely by advanced fighter aircraft and cruise missiles. They are increasingly shaped by layered attacks that combine drones, missiles, electronic warfare, and precision-guided weapons to exhaust defensive systems both physically and economically.
That lesson is already reshaping military procurement around the world. Governments are accelerating investment in dedicated counter-drone interceptors, electronic warfare, directed-energy weapons, and other lower-cost air-defense solutions that can defeat mass drone attacks without rapidly depleting expensive missile inventories.

title: US airlines tighten rules, ban humanoid robots from commercial flights
content:
A growing number of airlines in the US are banning humanoid robots from commercial flights, citing safety, handling, and operational concerns.
United Airlines and Delta Air Lines are the latest carriers to prohibit passengers from carrying humanoid robots in either cabin baggage or checked luggage.
The restrictions distinguish human-like robots from conventional consumer electronics and smaller robotic devices, which can still be transported under existing battery and baggage rules.
The moves follow similar action by Southwest Airlines earlier this year after a widely publicized incident involving a humanoid robot being transported on a commercial flight, highlighting emerging challenges for airlines.
Airlines are banning
robots from commercial flights as increasingly sophisticated machines raise new questions about how they should be screened, stored, and handled during air travel. United Airlines and Delta Air Lines are the latest carriers to prohibit passengers from transporting humanoid robots, expanding restrictions to both cabin and checked baggage.
United’s policy prohibits humanoid robots from being transported on its flights as carry-on baggage, checked luggage, or cargo. The airline’s guidance specifically identifies humanoid robots as prohibited items, placing them in a separate category from conventional consumer electronics and smaller robotic devices, reports

Delta Air Lines has adopted a similar policy, although it currently describes its ban as temporary. The airline does not accept
designed to resemble or imitate humans or animals in appearance, size, movement, or behavior as either carry-on or checked baggage. Delta’s restriction applies regardless of the robot’s size or intended purpose.
The policies do not appear to target robotics in general. Conventional devices such as robotic vacuum cleaners, toy robots, and other consumer electronics can still be transported when they meet existing baggage and lithium-battery requirements. Instead, the restrictions focus on humanoid and animal-like robots whose physical design and capabilities create transportation challenges that ordinary electronic devices do not.
Experts point out that the likely reason for the bans is the difficulty of applying existing aviation rules to increasingly advanced robots. Humanoid machines can have articulated arms and legs, unusual dimensions, heavy components, and large lithium-ion battery systems. Their shape and construction could make them harder to screen, secure, load, and store than conventional luggage.
Battery safety is another potential concern.
batteries are already subject to strict airline and aviation regulations because damaged, defective, or improperly handled batteries can create fire risks. A sophisticated humanoid robot may contain multiple batteries and complex electrical systems, making it more difficult for airline employees to determine how the machine should be transported and secured.
may also raise questions during boarding and emergencies. Their weight, mobility, articulated limbs, and unconventional shapes could create complications when being placed in overhead compartments, cargo holds, or other designated storage areas. Airlines may also need clear procedures for preventing a robot from shifting during flight or interfering with evacuation and emergency-response procedures.
The issue came into sharper focus earlier this year after a humanoid robot
aboard a Southwest Airlines flight. The incident drew attention to the lack of clear procedures for handling human-like robots and sparked discussion about their classification, seating, battery storage, and other transportation requirements. Southwest subsequently moved to prohibit humanoid and animal-like robots from its flights, becoming an earlier example of an airline establishing dedicated restrictions for this emerging category of technology.
The decisions by Southwest, United, and Delta suggest airlines are responding primarily to uncertainty around safety, handling, and regulatory compliance rather than to a known pattern of in-flight failures involving humanoid robots. As these machines become larger, more capable, and more common, airlines may increasingly develop specific rules to remove ambiguity for passengers, airport staff, and flight crews.

title: Researchers boost vacuum-deposited PSCs to 25.53% efficiency using acetate-driven crystallization control
content:
Researchers boost vacuum-deposited PSCs to 25.53% efficiency using acetate-driven crystallization control
Researchers from Nanjing Tech University have developed a vacuum-deposition strategy that improves the performance of fully evaporated perovskite solar cells (PSCs) by precisely controlling the solid-state reaction pathway during film formation.
Vacuum deposition is widely viewed as a scalable and solvent-free alternative to solution processing, with potential advantages for industrial integration. However, devices fabricated using this approach have historically lagged behind their solution-processed counterparts due to defects formed during crystallization. The Nanjing Tech team addressed this limitation by introducing formamidinium acetate as a reactive precursor that fundamentally alters how the perovskite phase forms.
The key mechanism lies in the direct reaction between formamidinium acetate and lead iodide (PbI
). “We find that formamidinium acetate reacts directly with PbI2 to form FAPbI3 seed layers, substantially lowering the barrier to the solid-state conversion of precursors into the crystalline δ-phase and their subsequent transformation into the α-phase perovskite.” These seed layers act as nucleation centers, effectively guiding crystal growth and enabling a more controlled transition from precursor materials to the final perovskite structure.
Devices fabricated using this approach achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.53%, placing them among the highest-performing vacuum-deposited PSCs reported to date. In addition, the cells exhibited an electroluminescence external quantum efficiency (EQE_EL) of 18.38%, indicating low non-radiative losses and efficient charge recombination dynamics.
The solvent-free nature of the process also contributed to strong operational stability. The devices retained over 95% of their initial PCE after 1,000 hours under the ISOS-L-1 protocol, highlighting the robustness of the resulting perovskite films.
This work demonstrates how engineering the reaction pathway at the precursor level can overcome long-standing limitations in vacuum-deposited perovskites. By combining seed-assisted crystallization with in situ defect passivation, the approach provides a viable route toward high-efficiency, scalable PSC manufacturing.

title: Researchers develop indium-free titanium oxynitride recombination layer for 33.3%-efficient perovskite-silicon tandems
content:
Researchers develop indium-free titanium oxynitride recombination layer for 33.3%-efficient perovskite-silicon tandems
Researchers from Soochow University, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University,
Suzhou Maxwell Technologies
, the University of Oxford, Wuxi EliTe Solar, Hangzhou Zhongneng Photoelectricity Technology, Shenzhen Polytechnic University and Suzhou National Laboratory have developed an indium-free recombination layer for monolithic perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells, based on titanium oxynitride (TiOxNy), reporting power conversion efficiencies of 33.3% on 1.0 cm² devices and 30.6% on industrial-size, 207.87 cm² tandems.
Monolithic perovskite/silicon tandems are widely seen as a route past the efficiency ceiling of single-junction photovoltaics, but turning lab-scale records into durable, manufacturable modules depends heavily on one thin layer: the recombination interconnect that joins the two subcells. That layer has to do three things at once - support fast charge recombination, stay optically transparent so light reaches both subcells, and form a chemically robust interface that holds up over time. Today's leading options each fall short somewhere: indium-containing transparent conductive oxides (TCOs) raise cost and supply concerns, while silicon-based tunnel junctions introduce parasitic optical losses.
The team's answer is to move away from both approaches and use conductive titanium oxynitride as a single, multifunctional recombination layer. TiOxNy is designed to support efficient vertical charge recombination between the perovskite and silicon subcells while suppressing lateral current leakage - a distinction that matters for long-term stability, since incomplete or inefficient recombination allows carriers to accumulate, degrading interfaces and accelerating performance loss during operation.
The material's role isn't purely electrical. TiOxNy also provides anchoring sites for self-assembled monolayers (SAMs), attaching through a tridentate binding configuration. Those SAMs help shape the energy landscape at the interface, improving contact selectivity and cutting down on recombination pathways that would otherwise waste photogenerated carriers. On the optical side, the layer is engineered to stay sufficiently transparent that both subcells can still harvest light efficiently - avoiding the usual trade-off between electrical performance and manufacturability.
Alongside the 33.3% and 30.6% PCE results, the devices showed improved operational durability, supporting the idea that TiOxNy stabilizes interfacial chemistry against the stresses that typically degrade tandem stacks, and not just their initial performance. Reaching 30.6% at 207.87 cm² is the more significant number for industrial translation: it suggests the recombination layer concept holds up under the structural and processing complexity of large-area fabrication, rather than being a lab-only effect confined to small test cells.
Being indium-free, with what the researchers describe as minimal optical penalty, TiOxNy is positioned as a scalable interconnection strategy for next-generation tandem photovoltaics. If the approach holds up across full manufacturing lines, it could help move perovskite-silicon tandems further from record-chasing lab devices and closer to high-yield, widely deployable production.

title: Algeria's solar market moves beyond potential - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A recent discussion hosted by the Middle East Solar Industry Association (MESIA) found the next phase of Algeria’s solar expansion will be shaped by gas economics, procurement design, grid readiness and whether the country can turn its 15 GW target into bankable projects.
Sol Soufan, MESIA
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
Image: Aboodi Vesakaran/Unsplash
Algeria’s solar story is often described through its resource potential: strong irradiation, large land availability, and proximity to Europe. Those fundamentals matter, but they are no longer the most useful way to assess the market. Most North African countries have good solar resources. The real question is whether those resources can be converted into bankable, grid-ready, and locally executable projects.
That was the central point emerging from MESIA’s recent discussion on Algeria’s solar market. Algeria is not facing the same transition logic as some of its neighbours. Morocco moved early partly because imported energy created a direct economic vulnerability. Tunisia is trying to split the burden between private generation and utility-led grid readiness. Algeria’s driver is different. Its gas is domestic, deeply linked to export value, and still central to the power system.
Boukhalfa Yaici, Director of Algeria Green Energy Cluster, framed the renewable transition as a question of energy sovereignty and economic logic rather than environmental preference alone. In his presentation, he noted that every megawatt-hour generated from solar or wind is a megawatt-hour of gas that can be preserved for export or higher-value industrial use. That distinction matters. Solar in Algeria is not simply a climate tool. It is a way to manage demand growth, protect gas value, diversify the power mix, and prepare for a more carbon-conscious export environment.
The scale of the challenge is clear. Algeria has set a 15 GW solar PV programme, with around 3.2 GW under implementation in southern and high-plateau provinces. The panel also noted that roughly 99% of electricity generation still comes from natural gas, while domestic electricity consumption continues to rise. This makes solar deployment less a question of ambition and more a question of pace, financing, and execution capacity.
The current market has largely developed through an EPC-led model, with Sonelgaz owning and financing projects before tendering construction. That approach can help move an initial pipeline, but it also places much of the financing burden on the public sector. If Algeria wants to move from gigawatts announced to gigawatts financed, independent power producer structures, long-term PPAs, and clearer offtake arrangements may become increasingly important. In other markets, private capital has moved faster where policy visibility, bankable contracts, competitive procurement, and credible counterparties reduced risk.
This is where Algeria’s solar opportunity becomes more complex. The issue is not whether modules are efficient enough or whether developers are interested. The issue is whether the enabling environment can support projects over 20- to 30-year lifetimes. Permitting, land access, grid connection approvals, transparent tenders, and local partnerships may sound procedural, but they are often the difference between a target and an investable market.
Grid readiness is another defining test. Large-scale solar cannot be planned separately from transmission, substations, storage, system monitoring, and demand-side flexibility. If grid infrastructure arrives late, renewable generation risks curtailment, and consumers ultimately pay through inefficiencies and delays. For Algeria, where some of the strongest resources are located far from major load centres, the grid is not a background issue. It is part of the project economics.
Battery storage is likely to move closer to the centre of the conversation. Panelists described storage not as an accessory, but as core infrastructure for higher solar penetration. Batteries can shift generation into periods of demand, provide voltage and frequency support, and help stabilise a system that will need more flexibility as variable renewables grow. In Algeria’s case, storage could also support industrial clean-energy zones, remote sites, and future PV-plus-storage applications in desert regions.
Technology selection will also need to be viewed through the full project lifecycle. In high-temperature, dusty, and in some areas humid conditions, module choice cannot be based only on peak efficiency. Degradation rates, temperature coefficients, bifacial performance, trackers, cleaning strategies, and long-term yield all feed into levelised cost of energy. The winners will not necessarily be those offering the lowest upfront cost, but those able to deliver reliable generation over decades.
Localization should be treated with the same discipline. Yaici’s presentation highlighted a 35% local content requirement and growing involvement from Algerian EPCs and suppliers in the current programme. But local content is not automatically industrial development. It becomes valuable when it builds repeatable capability: engineering know-how, workforce skills, component supply chains, manufacturing potential, and partnerships that survive beyond a single tender cycle.
Green hydrogen adds a longer-term strategic layer. GECA presented a future pathway in which renewable capacity could expand well beyond the 15 GW solar programme, with solar PV expected to remain the dominant technology. Yet hydrogen will not shortcut the early execution challenge. It depends on exactly the same foundations: low-cost renewable power, bankable structures, grid and export infrastructure, and sustained international cooperation.
Algeria’s solar market is therefore entering a more serious phase. The question is no longer whether the country has potential. It is whether that potential can be organised into a disciplined market. The next phase of solar in Algeria will not be defined by sunlight alone. It will be defined by whether projects are bankable, grid-aligned, storage-aware, and anchored in a local industrial base that can scale with the ambition.
Sol Soufan is Content and Digital Marketing Associate at the Middle East Solar Industry Association (MESIA).

title: As solar breaks records, its security must catch up - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
In May 2026, U.S. solar power hit a historic milestone by generating more electricity than coal for the first time, but rapid industry expansion brings critical security risks, particularly during construction, that require scalable and proactive physical defense strategies to protect valuable assets.
Jeremy White
Technology & Products
Utility-scale
Image: Pro-Vigil
, solar broke a record by doing something it had never done before in the United States: it generated more electricity than coal. According to data analyzed by energy think tank Ember, solar contributed 12.8% of the country’s electricity in May, beating out coal’s 12.2%. Additionally, solar became the third-largest source of power in the U.S., behind natural gas and nuclear.
Such a milestone provides a welcome stroke of validity to the industry. A win like this, though, measures capacity that’s already built, commissioned, and generating revenue. It doesn’t project the solar farms under construction or what the next broken record will look like. And it doesn’t say anything about whether the physical security plans for solar sites are keeping pace with how fast the industry is growing.
Solar buildout continues despite obstacles
The solar industry hasn’t experienced linear growth, and interruptions in policy can affect how the industry is set to continue growing.
According to the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA),
more than 450 solar and storage projects were bottlenecked by a slowdown in permitting.
Still, such numbers point to the industry’s sustained growth. The SEIA also projects continued growth in residential markets between 2027 and 2031.
On the ground, that means that many new construction sites across the country, starting from bare fields, will pop up for years to come. That’s the environment security planning must operate in: not after-the-fact reviews but in a forward-looking, preventative strategy, because growing industries often attract the roving eyes of thieves and vandals.
Protecting a site during construction
Often, the greatest exposure for a solar farm is during construction, before permanent power, fencing, and staff are in place. During this phase, equipment, panels, and copper wiring are sitting on an open site with little to slow a bad actor down.
The fence perimeter that will eventually circumvent a finished site (if implemented at all) is often not yet erected, or if it is, it only exists in sections, leaving the most theft-prone materials open to the elements and to the thieves hungry for a quick profit.
In May of this year
, a man was charged with stealing 2,000 feet of copper wiring and dozens of connectors from two solar farms in North Carolina after cutting through perimeter fencing. Losses on two different sites amounted to $11,000.
Traditional security measures for sites, such as fencing, lightning, and warning signage, all still matter, but their fail point is twofold: they’re designed for finished sites and they lack an additional preventative measure.
For remote solar sites
under construction, a comprehensive security strategy must exist before the panels and copper arrive. It can’t wait until the day the site goes live.
Rightsizing physical security
Scale presents a particular problem. Security plans designed for 10-acre solar farms don’t apply at 500 acres. They break. A handful of cameras and a light monitoring routine might be enough to adequately cover a 10-acre site, but if you multiply that footprint by fifty, the math doesn’t scale in a straight line. Camera count, monitoring load, and response protocols all have to be redesigned, not simply expanded.
Ten times the perimeter doesn’t mean you need ten times the cameras. It means you need a monitoring approach that can still distinguish a legitimate, after-hours technician from an intruder on a site of that size. And you still need to be able to respond in seconds rather than minutes or more.
Proactive security that grows with the site
Often, many businesses won’t invest in a proactive security strategy until an incident resulting in monetary loss forces their hand. A truly proactive security strategy is
a layered one
. In practice, that means combining multiple tools, technologies, and obstacles to create a robust system that not only catches thieves in action but
them and prevents crime.
This can start with perimeter fences and incorporates cameras. In today’s security, monitored units are preferable to simple record-and-store cameras. Video surveillance tools can either be
(for sites with ready access to internet, places with brick-and-mortar buildings) or
(which are better for remote areas that lack access to Wi-Fi).
For solar farms, mobile surveillance units tend to work better as they provide connected access for remote areas and can be moved to support a continuously evolving strategy. Because they don’t require permanent power or wiring, mobile surveillance units can accompany a solar site at any stage: from the early days of construction through to daily operation once construction is complete and the site is in full swing.
As the project’s surface area expands during construction, additional mobile units can be deployed to keep eyes on the riskiest entry points simultaneously.
But it’s what occurs on the other side of those camera lenses that turns a reactive security strategy into a proactive one. Mobile surveillance units are equipped with
AI-powered detection
which is trained to distinguish between an access-permitted contractor and a would-be thief cutting through the fence line.
When detection is escalated for a threat, a trained human monitor confirms that a threat is in fact on the premises, and they can cue
audio and visual deterrents
to ward off the thief.
As a site grows, having this layered strategy ensures a methodical and pragmatic approach to a solar farm’s physical security, helping to deter thieves
they intend to act. And when a site is complete and fully operational, a layered security strategy helps to prevent damage, theft, and loss.
Solar overtaking coal in May was a big moment, and it’s a clue into the growth the industry is set to experience. As the industry continues to expand, the target on its back grows as well. With projects set to take place, the time to invest in a proactive security strategy is before the project breaks ground, not after an incident occurs.

title: Australia adds over 700 MW of rooftop solar in April-June - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
More than 700 MW of rooftop solar was added to Australia’s main grid in the past three months, helping drive wholesale electricity prices in the country’s National Electricity Market to their lowest June quarter average since 2020.
David Carroll
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Solar Victoria
Australia’s cumulative rooftop solar capacity in its National Electricity Mark (NEM) increased from 25.7 GW as of the
first quarte
r of 2026 to 26.4 GW by the end of the June quarter (Q2 2026), according to a report published by the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO). The total covers 3.9 million installations.
AEMO’s latest
Quarterly Energy Dynamics report
also shows household battery energy storage capacity across the NEM grew by almost 3.3 GWh or 41% during Q2 2026.
The report also notes 14 new grid-scale generation and storage projects totalling 3.9 GW of capacity reached full output during Q2 2026, double the previous quarterly record. This comprised 2.7 GW of battery capacity, 0.5 GW of solar-plus-battery capacity, 0.4 GW of solar capacity and 0.2 GW of wind capacity.
These supply changes lifted the renewable share of NEM generation to a new Q2 high of 42.1%, up from 37.1% in the same period last year.
Distributed PV output reached a record Q2 average of 2,520 MW, up 6.9% year-on-year, increasing its share of the energy mix to 10.3% for the quarter. Grid-scale solar generation increased by 12% to average 1,860 MW, with its share increasing to 7.6% from 6.8%, while wind output increased by 20% to 4,198 MW.
Coal generation fell 5% year-on-year to 13,158 MW, while gas-powered generation dropped 30% to its lowest Q2 average since 2003, at 1,050 MW, 30% lower than in Q2 2025.
AEMO said the record share of renewables drove average wholesale electricity prices in the NEM to their lowest June quarter average since 2020, down 47% from the same period last year to an average of AUD 74 ($51.58)/MWh.
AEMO Executive General Manager Policy and Corporate Affairs, Violette Mouchaileh, said continued investment in renewables and storage is reshaping the market. “These technologies are changing demand patterns, supporting system reliability and increasing the amount of lower-cost energy available across the market,” she said.
The same was not true for Western Australia, where the renewable share of generation declined from 33.6% to 32% for the quarter. Rooftop solar output in the Wholesale Electricity Market (WEM) increased by 3.4% but wind generation decreased by 13% due in part to lower wind speeds, while coal-fired generation fell by 17% reflecting planned and forced outages.
AEMO said these reductions increased reliance on gas-fired generation, which rose by 27%, driving average real-time wholesale electricity prices up 30% year-on-year to AUD 118/MWh.

title: Chile forecasts up to 58 GW of new solar capacity by 2057 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Chile’s Ministry of Energy has presented its preliminary long-term energy plan, which anticipates between 27 GW and 58 GW of new solar capacity over the next 30 years across five different growth scenarios.
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Elias Almaguer/Unsplash
Chile could install between 27 GW and 58 GW of new photovoltaic capacity over the next 30 years, according to the Ministry of Energy’s
Preliminary Report of the Long-Term Energy Planning (PELP) 2028-2032
The range covers five different scenarios featured in the report that are influenced by differing trajectories of economic growth, fuel costs, technological evolution, and energy policies. The model is based on an existing solar capacity of 12,015 MW, covering both large-scale plants and small distributed generation facilities. An additional 490 MW of installations under the net billing scheme are also included, directly deducted from the demand in the modeling.
The projections included in the report will serve as input toward the annual transmission expansion plans prepared by the country’s National Energy Commission. The document also projects an expansion of between 16 GW and 27 GW of onshore wind energy.
Northern solar power is expanding along with batteries
Across all five scenarios, the optimal expansion of the National Electric System relies primarily on new photovoltaic solar energy in the north of the country and on land-based wind farms in the Maule and Biobío regions in central-southern Chile.
Photovoltaic development appears to be associated with the incorporation of battery energy storage systems, especially in scenarios that contemplate higher fossil fuel prices, the retirement of coal-fired power plants and the inclusion of a carbon dioxide tax in the variable costs of generation.
The model uses as a starting point 4,078 MW of BESS systems installed or under construction by the end of 2026, with an average storage duration of 4.3 hours. Most of this capacity is located in the north: 56% in Antofagasta, 15% in Atacama and another 15% in Tarapacá.
The report identifies a need for longer-lasting storage systems for new investments. Several scenarios in the report include six- and eight-hour solutions as a significant portion of the expansion, due to the need to shift solar generation to nighttime hours and provide flexibility during periods of lower solar irradiance.
Batteries are the only storage technology that the model incorporates as new capacity during the planning horizon, with no expansion of pumped hydro storage, thermal storage, or other emerging technologies included.
The report also analyzes offshore wind energy for the first time. This technology is developed in three of the five scenarios, provided its costs register a medium or favorable reduction. Its earliest implementation occurs in 2041, while in other scenarios it appears from 2048 onwards.
Towards the end of the projected timeframe, at least 83% of annual electricity generation would come from solar photovoltaic or wind power. Renewable curtailments would account for between 9% and 12% of generation, compared to the 7% used as a baseline for the current situation.
Transmission reinforcements at 500 kV and 220 kV
The expansion of renewable energy will require new investments in transmission. The report identifies the need to increase the capacity of the Charrúa-Ancoa-Alto Jahuel-Lo Aguirre corridor by at least 1,750 MVA, at 500 kV. This reinforcement would allow wind power generation to be transported from the south-central region to the main consumption areas and to the north, via the future Kimal-Lo Aguirre line.
The plan also includes expansions of Chile’s 220 kV networks. Some lines would need to increase their current capacity up to six times in all the scenarios studied. The greatest needs are concentrated in the Antofagasta and Maule regions in north-central Chile.
Energy demand increases by up to 47.8%
The scenarios project national energy demand growth of between 4.1% and 47.8% during the analyzed period. The outcome depends primarily on the evolution of the gross domestic product and the degree of electrification of the economy.
Transportation remains the largest energy consumer, while regulatory scenarios anticipate increased adoption of electric cars, taxis, and buses, as well as the use of hydrogen in heavy transport.
Mining and industry are also increasing their electricity consumption, while data centers are emerging as a new structural source of demand. The report estimates data center capacity at 198 MW in 2024, which could reach approximately 594 MW in 2030 and 900 MW in 2057.
Individuals and institutions registered in the PELP process may submit comments on the report until August 24. The ministry will then prepare a final report and, after a further review, the corresponding energy planning decree.

title: Fire at Spanish solar plant burns 90 hectares - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The fire, which broke out last Wednesday afternoon, left one worker injured with burns. The cause of the fire is yet to be reported.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
Applications & Installations
The fire was captured by the Castilla-La Mancha Forest Fire Information System (InfoCam) | Image: InfoCam
A fire at a photovoltaic plant located in the municipality of Puertollano, central Spain, affected around 90 hectares and forced the deployment of a large firefighting operation.
According to the mayor of Puertollano, Miguel Ángel Ruiz, the fire originated in one of the large photovoltaic installations located next to the N-420 highway. The first warning was issued by the company operating the plant itself.
The fire broke out around 13:00 last Wednesday (July 22). At the time, three workers were on site and attempted to contain the fire. A 51-year old man suffered burns and required initial treatment from a mobile intensive care unit before being airlifted by helicopter to Getafe Hospital.
The cause of the fire has not yet been reported. The relevant authorities will need to determine whether it originated from electrical equipment, components of the photovoltaic plant, or other external factors.
Minister of Sustainable Development for the region of Castilla-La Mancha, Mercedes Gómez, explained that the fire was already contained and under control by Thursday morning and stressed that one of the main objectives of the intervention was to prevent the flames from reaching nearby industrial facilities and to guarantee the safety of the surrounding area.
The flames did not significantly reach the forest mass of the Dehesa Boyal park, one of the main natural areas near the city.
A total eight aircrafts and up to 24 ground vehicles participated in the firefighting efforts, mobilizing up to 129 people, including forest firefighters, environmental agents and support personnel.
Throughout Thursday, several ground teams remained in the area carrying out cooling operations to prevent possible flare-ups of the fire.

title: Mexican graduates develop agrivoltaic system with rainwater harvesting, smart irrigation - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The group’s agrivoltaic proposal, known as SolarRoot, integrates photovoltaics with crops, rainwater harvesting and subsurface drip irrigation controlled by moisture sensors.
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
SolarRoot system diagram | Image: Monterrey Institute of Technology
A team of recent graduates from the School of Engineering and Sciences at the Monterrey Institute of Technology have developed a novel agrivoltaic proposal.
Known as SolarRoot, their system combines photovoltaic modules installed above the crops with rainwater harvesting and an underground drip irrigation network. Soil moisture sensors determine when irrigation is necessary and allow only the required volume of water to be supplied to the plants.
The proposal also seeks to utilize the shade cast by solar panels to reduce heat stress on crops and minimize water loss. According to its developers, the goal of SolarRoot is to produce electricity and food without dedicating separate areas to each activity.
The institute has not disclosed the planned photovoltaic power output, the type or number of modules, the required surface area, the crops that would be used, or the amount of water that could be recovered. The project remains a engineering proposal under evaluation, with any planned construction of a pilot project yet to be announced.
SolarRoot won first place in an international competition, Invent for the Planet, promoted by the College of Engineering at Texas A&M University. The competition involves 48-hour workshops in which university teams develop solutions to challenges related to energy, the environment, resource equity, and social development.
The project will now represent the graduates’ Mexico City campus in the next stage of the competition. Projects that pass that stage will advance to the final phase of the competition, scheduled to take place in Qatar.

title: OCI Holdings plans to double polysilicon production capacity by 2029 - pv magazine Global
content: Seoul-headquartered chemicals company OCI Holdings says it is planning to expand its annual polysilicon production capacity from 35,000 metric tons to 70,000 by 2029. The company says the planned expansion is geared towards meeting demand from the US artificial intelligence infrastructure and space industries. In April this year, it was reported that Malaysia’s OCI TerraSus, a subsidiary of OCI Holdings, was in talks with SpaceX over a multi-year polysilicon supply contract . OCI’s latest update adds that it has established and is operating a US-bound non-prohibited foreign entity (PFE) solar supply chain that links OCI TerraSus and Vietnam wafer manufacturer NeoSilicon Technology (NST). OCI Holdings is the majority shareholder and primary material supplier of NST, having acquired a 65% stake in the company in October 2025. NST is planning to expand its production capacity from around 2.7 GW today to 11.5 GW by 2029, with supply to the U.S. market anticipated to begin next year. “With the expansion of AI data centers, the growth momentum of solar power in the US energy market is further strengthening,” commented OCI Holdings chairman Lee Woo-hyun. “Based on our differentiated non-PFE competitiveness, we will expand investment in the solar value chain and proactively respond to changes in the global supply chain.” Earlier this year, OCI TerraSus secured a $125 million A Loan from the International Finance Corporation for a semiconductor-grade polysilicon production facility in Sarawak, Malaysia, billed as the first of its kind in southeast Asia. title: Solmeria opens platform for buying solar, storage projects - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The French company, formerly known as Ferme Solaire, launched the new marketplace for buying and selling solar and storage projects in Europe earlier this month.
François Puthod
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Pixabay
French renewables company Solmeria, formerly known as Ferme Solaire, has launched a European-wide platform for selling solar and battery energy storage system (BESS) projects directly to buyers.
Known as Solmeria Marketplace, the platform spans ground-mounted PV, agriPV, C&I solar and BESS, at all stages of development ranging from greenfield to ready-to-build projects.
The commission, payable only upon successful completion of a sale, is significantly lower than that of a traditional merger and acquisitions agency.
Created at the request of developers, the marketplace is aiming to bring liquidity to all projects, accelerate transactions and reduce intermediation costs.
The marketplace launched in early July. Maxime Curtaigne, CEO of Solmeria, told
pv magazine France
there are already 28 developers registered on the platform.
There are currently 24 projects listed, all at differing stages of development, totaling 200 MW of capacity. Several hundered MWs of projects are expected by the end of the year.
“Developers know how to sell a project, but they waste considerable time finding the right buyer, and end up grouping everything into a portfolio at the expense of their best assets. We want to reverse this logic: make each project marketable individually and connect it with the person who will give it its true value,” Curtaigne explained.
“Value is not in the portfolio, it is in the relevant connection. Solmeria wants to become the infrastructure for this new liquidity in the European solar market,” he adds.

title: Taiwan introduces new solar rules for large buildings - pv magazine Global
content: Taiwan is set to bring in new rules governing the installation of solar PV systems on large buildings. From August 1, amendments to Taiwan’s Renewable Energy Development Act will require newly constructed, expanded or renovated buildings with a floor area of 1,000 square metres or more to install solar PV systems at a rate of 1 kW per 20 square metres of building area. During a briefing on the new regulations, Deputy Minister of Taiwan’s Ministry of the Interior (MOI), Dong Jian-hong, said the rules are expected to add around 660 MW of solar PV capacity annually. A news release from the MOI and Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) said the requirements will help increase the supply of green energy in urban areas while improving the energy independence and resilience of buildings with solar. The updated regulations also require solar installations to be incorporated into building plans from the design stage. This approach aims to balance aesthetics, practicality and safety, while reducing the construction and management challenges associated with adding solar systems after buildings have been completed, the ministries said. The MOI added that it will work with MOEA’s Energy Administration, Taiwan Power Company, and industry stakeholders to establish coordination mechanisms between building designers and the solar industry. The collaboration will aim to address any concerns related to equipment design, maintenance management and grid connections. “The aim is to gradually develop a comprehensive process covering solar PV planning, installation, grid connection and subsequent maintenance management, providing the industry with the necessary professional support,” the ministries said. Taiwan is on track to more than double its current solar capacity by the end of 2035, according to analysis by consultancy GlobalData, with forecasted annual growth additions between 1 GW and 2 GW. In May, the city of Taoyuan in northern Taiwan published local guidelines for solar power projects in a move signalling a shift towards a regionalized approach for solar permitting in the country. The announcement followed changes to Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan on national-level regulations governing the development of ground-mounted and floating solar projects that followed a major typhoon in July 2025, damaging over 135,000 solar panels .
